problem: If $f(x,y)=xy+x{e}^{y},$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y)$ from $(2,0)$ to $(1,-0.5).$
worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =(y+{e}^{y})\,\text{d}x+(x+x{e}^{y})\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(2,0),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(2,0) & =(0+{e}^{0})\,\text{d}x+(2+2\cdot {e}^{0})\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+4\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(2+Δx,0+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈1\,Δx+4\,Δy.
$$

Moving from $(2,0)$ to $(1,-0.5),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1-2=-1, \\ Δy & =-0.5-0=-0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\,Δx+4\,Δy \\  & ≈1\cdot (-1)+4\cdot (-0.5) \\  & ≈-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ decreases by approximately $3.$
